language: English; original Bangla names included when explicitly known
purpose: Codex-ready seed dataset for a Bangladesh cultural/natural/historical/food/handicraft discovery platform such as ShilpoHub
scope_notice: COMPILATION, NOT AN EXHAUSTIVE INVENTORY. Includes earlier craft research (all table rows), all named heritage sites/themes in the ongoing conversation, Faridpur regional products and Bhola buffalo curd. Certain wider categories and landmark names are seeds rather than individually researched entries. Absence of a district item is not evidence that it has no heritage.

source_and_verification_rules.record_status: source_backed = prior source or official verification; needs_research/name_only/seed = discussed but detailed source research is incomplete.
source_and_verification_rules.history_null: Unknown/unresearched. Never replace with generated lore.
source_and_verification_rules.location_rules: Preserve source text; name splitting by comma is conservative, slash names may be alternate spellings OR combined localities. Review before geo-coding.
source_and_verification_rules.upazila_rules: When upazila_or_area contains /, region, district, belt, city or town, do NOT assume it is one validated administrative upazila.
source_and_verification_rules.coordinate_rules: All coordinates are null because no site-level geocoding was verified in this compilation.
source_and_verification_rules.factuality_rules: Counts and dates in news are historical snapshots and should not be used as current figures without rechecking.
source_and_verification_rules.recognition_rules: Official UNESCO inscription differs from GI; do not infer UNESCO recognition or GI registration from product popularity.
source_and_verification_rules.source_policy: Sources preserve prior document URLs; rechecked_in_current_run is true only for targeted September 2026 web checks. Prior sources were not all re-reviewed in this turn.
source_and_verification_rules.future_enrichment: When a district has a zero record count or a place history is null, research that district/place rather than inventing missing records.
source_and_verification_rules.named_locality_rules: craft_named_locality_records is an extraction aid, not a validated gazetteer. A comma separates localities only when the source text allows it; locality_role does not assert village status. Slash-combined places are not silently treated as single villages.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Fine patterned handloom fabric traditionally associated with the historic Dhaka textile region.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Motifs are woven into the cloth by hand using supplementary weft rather than printed afterwards.
heritage_items.history: The historic Dhaka weaving region became renowned for patterned fine cloth during the Mughal era. Jamdani production survived in the Narayanganj/Rupganj weaving belt despite later industrial competition.
materials_or_ingredients: Silk yarn in some contemporary products

heritage_items.what_it_is: Historic extremely fine cotton textile associated with the Dhaka region.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Historically celebrated for unusually delicate handspun yarn and fine weaving.
heritage_items.history: Fine Dhakai muslin became internationally celebrated in the early modern period and later suffered major decline. Revival initiatives exist, but historic production should not be treated as a continuously operating village industry.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Traditional handwoven saree associated with Tangail weaving communities.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Fine cloth and detailed regional woven designs.
heritage_items.history: Tangail handloom traditions span multiple villages; the saree tradition has formal UNESCO intangible-heritage recognition since 2025.

unesco_ich.element: Traditional Saree weaving art of Tangail

heritage_items.what_it_is: Tangail handloom industry making sarees alongside dhoti, lungi, gamcha and related cloth.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Different Tangail villages specialise in different handwoven products.
heritage_items.history: The Tangail district government documents a long-established multi-village weaving belt and its product specialisations.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Decorative hand-stitched quilts and textile articles particularly associated with Jamalpur.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Coloured embroidered motifs expressing rural life and storytelling; livelihoods for village women.
heritage_items.history: Nakshi Kantha is a wider Bengali tradition; Jamalpur developed an important specialised commercial hand-embroidery identity.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Decorative stitched quilts and embroidered cloth made in many regions of Bangladesh.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Regional motifs, layered cloth and hand stitching.
heritage_items.history: An inherited Bengali textile practice found across multiple districts; its geographical spread is broader than the Jamalpur commercial identity.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Traditional silk textile associated with Rajshahi and nearby silk weaving areas.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Silk yarn woven into fine clothing and accessories.
heritage_items.history: The Rajshahi region developed a major silk production and weaving identity linked to local sericulture and textile craftsmanship.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Traditional handwoven flat floor-rug associated with Rangpur.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Distinctive local patterns and weaving using textile fibres.
heritage_items.history: Rangpur is strongly associated with Shataranji production; Nishbetganj is an identified craft centre.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Cool-feeling traditional mats made with split and processed murta cane.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Detailed handweaving and strong family transmission of skills.
heritage_items.history: The greater-Sylhet Shital Pati practice was inscribed by UNESCO in 2017; production is also found outside Sylhet.

unesco_ich.element: Traditional art of Shital Pati weaving of Sylhet

heritage_items.what_it_is: Woven traditional cool mat, commonly made from murta strips.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Smooth decorative handweaving and traditional household use.
heritage_items.history: Shital Pati craft extends beyond the Sylhet UNESCO-inscribed tradition to other Bangladeshi districts.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Traditional hand fan made from palmyra palm leaves.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Hand processing, weaving and decorative painting varies by village.
heritage_items.history: Seasonal family craft traditions survive in several districts, including Faridpur, Rajbari, Barishal, Bogura and Natore.
materials_or_ingredients: Bamboo/wood for handle in some forms

heritage_items.what_it_is: Household and decorative articles woven from hogla reed leaves.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Natural-fibre weaving based on local wetland plant resources.
heritage_items.history: Documented modern clusters include Anandanagar in Khulna and Tiakhali in Barishal.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Handmade clay vessels, toys and ritual/decorative pottery.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Craft-specific shapes, handwork and firing techniques within traditional potter settlements.
heritage_items.history: Pottery has long been widespread; old BSCIC mapping recorded hundreds of pottery villages, not a complete modern active village register.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Decorative painted art associated with Dhaka rickshaws.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Bright folk-inspired images on working urban vehicles.
heritage_items.history: Dhaka rickshaws and rickshaw painting were inscribed on UNESCO’s intangible cultural heritage list in 2023.

unesco_ich.element: Rickshaws and rickshaw painting in Dhaka

heritage_items.what_it_is: Hereditary design and construction of traditional wooden boats.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Craft knowledge adapted to riverine transport and local water conditions.
heritage_items.history: Traditional boatmaking is documented in a heritage inventory for Gopalganj; it should not be treated as an already inscribed UNESCO element.

recognition.unesco_nomination_note: Referenced by UNESCO as a pending-priority file, not an inscription.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Traditional handwoven clothing and textiles made by Manipuri weaving households.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Community-specific dress, shawls and weaving practices.
heritage_items.history: An inherited craft practised in several Kamalganj-area villages of Moulvibazar.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Traditional Rakhine weaving, including clothing, scarves and bags.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Culturally distinctive products and intergenerational household skill.
heritage_items.history: Rakhine weaving remains documented in some southern coastal communities, while reports also describe declining practice in some areas.

Raw jute fibre produced in Faridpur, a major jute-growing district of Bangladesh.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Jute is the region's iconic 'golden fibre', supporting farming and fibre-based rural work.
heritage_items.history: Long-established crop and regional economic identity linked with the riverine agricultural landscape; official GI recognition is recorded by DPDT.
heritage_items.importance_note: District-level production; individual producing villages not comprehensively enumerated in earlier discussion.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Winter molasses made by concentrating fresh sap collected from date-palm trees.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Seasonal aroma and flavour; served with traditional pitha, rice dishes and snacks.
heritage_items.history: Date-palm tapping (gachhi work) is part of winter rural food and agricultural tradition in Faridpur; these localities had documented producers in a recent report.
traditional_methods: Overnight sap collection in hanging pots
Boiling sap to produce liquid or solid molasses
heritage_items.importance_note: The cited report documents these particular localities; the craft is district-wide.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Soft chhana-based syrup-soaked rasgulla associated with a long-running sweet shop.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Soft texture, relatively light sweetness and pronounced fresh-chhana flavour.
heritage_items.history: The Tetultola shop dates to around 1950 and is traditionally associated with founder Sheikh Sabdar Hossain and later Jahurul Haque, known as Khoka Mia. News accounts differ in some family succession details; only the shared high-level founding history is retained.
heritage_items.importance_note: Shop/local food heritage, not a geographical indication.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Local sweet-selling area that developed around Tetultola rasgulla.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Historic association with Khoka Mia’s sweet shop and neighbouring shops.
heritage_items.history: Locality became associated with rasgulla production and sale following a shop established about 1950.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Seasonal traditional market supplying wooden boats used in waterlogged agricultural areas.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Connects monsoon boatcraft, jute-retting and farming livelihoods.
heritage_items.history: Earlier reporting described this market as roughly a century old; the approximate age is an attribution, not an independently verified founding date.

heritage_items.what_it_is: Traditional fermented raw buffalo-milk curd, typically set in earthen pots.
heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Rich, thick texture and distinctive tart flavour; traditionally served during family occasions and festivals.
heritage_items.history: Local reporting describes an approximately 200-year-old buffalo-curd tradition connected to Bhola charland buffalo-rearing households.
traditional_methods: Traditional fermentation and setting in earthen containers
techniques: Traditional fermentation and setting in earthen containers

heritage_items.what_makes_it_special: Connects deltaic islands, animal husbandry and traditional food heritage.

nationwide_craft_context.description: Nakshi Kantha is made across Bangladesh rather than belonging to a single district. Banglapedia historically notes particularly important traditions in Rajshahi, Chapainawabganj, Rangpur, Faridpur and Kushtia, while other sources and GI documentation add Jamalpur/Mymensingh, Bogura, Jashore and Chattogram among notable regions. The basic process uses old or layered cotton cloth with coloured thread, especially running/kantha stitches, with floral, geometric, animal, village-life and narrative motifs. For a database, do not label "Nakshi Kantha = Jamalpur only". Jamalpur is a major commercial/GI identity, but the craft itself is geographically much wider. (S68, S67, S31)

This is one of the least realistic categories for a supposedly complete online village list. Historic BSCIC mapping counted 1,154 bamboo/cane craft villages - more than a quarter of the 4,226 craft villages it mapped. Products include baskets, trays, stools, chairs, tables, swings, fish traps, storage containers, household utensils, decorative ware and bags. Major raw-material regions include Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, the Chittagong Hill Tracts and Sylhet, although artisans work throughout Bangladesh. (S69)

Older BSCIC mapping counted approximately 666 pottery villages, so Bijoypur, Rayerbazar, Madanpura, Champaknagar and Kartikpur are important named centres, not the only places making pottery. Products include hari/pots, pitchers, plates, bowls, doi-sora, lamps, toys, dolls, elephants, horses, masks, idols, terracotta plaques, flowerpots and painted ritual pottery. (S13)

Jute craft occurs broadly in Dhaka, Mymensingh and Tangail, among other areas. Traditional techniques include braiding into beni, making dori/twine, and constructing shika, bags, plant hangers, baskets and decorative objects; modern producers add macrame, home decor, toys and accessories. (S70)

Important documented regions include Manikganj, Keraniganj/Dhaka, Munshiganj, Cumilla, Brahmanbaria, Kishoreganj, Netrokona, Moulvibazar, Habiganj, Jamalpur, Sherpur, Jashore, Rangpur, Dinajpur and Barishal, plus specifically documented artisans in Hazrahati, Magura and Arpara, Kushtia. Products include wedding ornaments, religious decor, crowns, flowers, dolls, birds, animals and festival decorations. (S17)

This deserves its own craft category rather than being hidden under bamboo craft. Verified production villages/localities in this directory include Chandshi (Barishal), Joynagar (Faridpur), Kestopur (Rajbari), Tekpara/Sutrodhar Para/Malpara in Nikli (Kishoreganj), Arola-Jogirbhaban (Bogura), Hapania (Natore), and Mansa (Bagerhat). (S47, S11, S16, S14, S37, S38, S43)

At least two particularly clear modern clusters are Anandanagar, Terokhada, Khulna and Tiakhali/Hogla Palli, Barishal city. Hogla leaves are dried and woven into mats, baskets, ropes, screens/fences and roofing material. (S39, S48)

UNESCO recognises the traditional art of Shital Pati weaving of Sylhet, made from strips of murta cane, with family-based knowledge transmission and particularly strong participation by women. The tradition extends across greater Sylhet and also occurs in southern and central Bangladesh. (S58)
